w: Cut straight into a cliff in 1923-24, this mining harbour let ore slide down chutes bored through solid rock and drop onto waiting ships, skipping the old cart-and-barge relay. Engineer Cesare Vecelli named it after his own daughter Flavia - a personal touch on a genuinely unique piece of engineering.
s: A mining harbour cut straight into the cliff
_facts: Sea harbour near Nebida, Iglesias comune, South Sardinia, built 1923-24
Served as the mineral production hub for the Masua mine on the Iglesiente coast
Named after Flavia Vecelli, daughter of the harbour's engineer Cesare Vecelli
Considered a unique and outstanding engineering feat for its time

w: A stepped stone platform rising out of open farmland near Sassari, raised as an altar by the Ozieri culture as early as 4000 BC - centuries before Stonehenge's first stones went up. Nobody fully agrees on what rites took place on top of it, which is part of the pull.
_facts: Neolithic archaeological site in the territory of Sassari, northern Sardinia
A massive raised stone platform thought to have been an altar
Built by the Ozieri culture or earlier, oldest parts dated to around 4000-3650 BC

w: Eight kilometres of sand running from the cliff known as the Devil's Saddle to the edge of Quartu Sant'Elena, with the Molentargius-Saline salt-pan reserve backing onto it. It's less a single beach than Cagliari's whole social calendar, laid out along the water.
_facts: Main beach of Cagliari, stretching about 8km
Runs from Sella del Diavolo (Devil's Saddle) to the Quartu Sant'Elena coastline
Backs onto the Molentargius-Saline Regional Park

n: Arcipelago di La Maddalena National Park
w: A scatter of granite islands and 180km of protected coastline off Sardinia's northern tip - and, until 2020, home to exactly one resident. Mauro Morandi moved into a derelict WWII shelter on Budelli in 1989 and stayed three decades as its self-appointed caretaker, before the park authorities finally evicted him.
s: An archipelago with one very stubborn resident
_facts: Geomarine national park established 1994, over 12,000 hectares of land and sea, 180km of coast
Covers the islands of La Maddalena, Caprera, Spargi, Budelli, Razzoli, Santa Maria and others
Mauro Morandi lived alone on Budelli island in a former WWII shelter from 1989
Described as the park's unofficial caretaker; evicted by the end of 2020

w: An uninhabited island known for its scattered Roman-era wreck debris - and, briefly in 2008, the self-declared site of a Sardinian nationalist micronation. Neither claim changed much about the place, which remains empty and quietly strange.
s: Roman wrecks and a one-day micronation
_facts: Island off the coast of Sardinia, Sardinian name Malu 'Entu
Notable for Roman ruins
Site of a Sardinian nationalist attempt to create a micronation in 2008

w: Whoever ruled Sardinia on behalf of its absentee king - Aragonese, then Spanish, then Savoy - governed from this palace in Cagliari's old Castello district. The crown moved on centuries ago; the building never really changed jobs, and now houses the Metropolitan City administration instead.
s: Where Sardinia's absentee king was represented
_facts: Also known as the Viceregio (Viceroyal Palace), in Cagliari's historic Castello district
Official residence of the King of Sardinia's representative under Aragonese, Spanish and Savoy rule
Today serves as the seat of the Metropolitan City of Cagliari

w: Three basalt towers rise out of the Campidano plain, but the real draw is underfoot: Monte Arci was one of Sardinia's key obsidian sources, mined for tools and weapons since prehistoric times and traded off the island long before anyone wrote any of it down.
_facts: Isolated volcanic massif in the Uras plain, Campidano, south-western Sardinia, highest point 812m
Composed of three basalt towers with a trachyte core
Abundant obsidian mined here since prehistoric times, used for tools and weapons and traded off-island
Also has pearlite quarries

w: Excavated since 1909, this hilltop sanctuary near Serri turned out to be the richest Nuragic site dug up so far - bronze bull figurines, nuraghe models, votive weapons, pointing to a shrine used from the Bronze Age through Punic, Roman and Byzantine times, until a fire (the ash layer is still there) ended it.
s: The richest Nuragic shrine ever dug up
_facts: Archaeological site in Serri, named for a Romanesque church built over a Roman-era place of worship
In use from the Middle Bronze Age (1600-1300 BC), most important Nuragic complex excavated to date
Finds include bronze bull protomes, stylized nuraghe models, votive weapons and ex-voto figurines
Excavations began in 1909 led by Antonio Taramelli
Ash layer suggests a fire in Roman times devastated the site; coins show continuity into the medieval period

w: A flat-topped mesa above Siligo, crowned with the church of St Elias and St Enoch - a summit chapel old enough to be named in an 11th-century donation list sent to the abbey of Montecassino by a local judge, Barisone I of Torres.
s: A mesa-top chapel named in an 11th-century deed
_facts: Isolated mountain and mesa in Logudoro, Sassari province, elevation 733m, mostly in Siligo's territory
Summit plateau holds the church of St Elias and St Enoch
Named in an 11th-century gift list to the abbey of Montecassino from Judge Barisone I of Torres

w: A quiet stone church out in the countryside near Siligo, its name - Our Lady of Mesumundu - about the only clue left to whatever devotion first raised it here. No grand facts survive, just a small, plain building that has outlasted whoever built it.
s: A lone countryside church near Siligo
_facts: Religious building in the territory of Siligo, Sardinia
Name translates as 'Our Lady of Mesumundu'

w: Twenty kilometres outside Cagliari, this working astronomical observatory has been quietly tracking the wobble of the Earth's own rotation since 1899 - a niche, patient kind of science, still going.
_facts: Astronomical observatory owned and operated by Italy's INAF, 20km from Cagliari
Founded in 1899 to study the Earth's rotation

w: One of the many nuraghi scattered across South Sardinia's interior, standing quietly in the countryside near Villanovafranca - Bronze Age engineering that has outlasted every empire that later passed through.
s: A Bronze Age tower in the Sardinian interior
_facts: Archaeological site (nuraghe) in the territory of Villanovafranca, South Sardinia province

w: Built directly over a two-mouthed cave on a limestone plateau between Osini and Gairo, this Bronze Age complex packs a 6.3-metre central tower, three smaller ones and eight round huts around a single courtyard - engineering wrapped around a natural void nobody fully explains.
s: A nuraghe built over a two-mouthed cave
_facts: Nuragic complex dating to the 18th-10th century BC, in the municipality of Osini, Ogliastra
Built over a cave with two entrances, on a limestone plateau between Osini and Gairo
Central tower 6.3m high flanked by three smaller towers, surrounded by 8 circular huts
Access to the towers through a small courtyard; used from Early to Late Bronze Age

w: Sardinia's wildest corner holds its highest peak, Punta La Marmora, plus a wildlife list most parks would envy - mouflon, golden eagles, the near-mythical Mediterranean monk seal patrolling the coast below. Wildcats and dormice found nowhere else round out a park still genuinely feral in places.
_facts: National park on Sardinia's east coast, in the provinces of Nuoro and Ogliastra
Contains Punta La Marmora, the highest mountain in Sardinia
Wildlife includes the Sardinian wildcat, mouflon, marten, Sardinian fox, golden and Bonelli's eagles
Marine life includes the Mediterranean monk seal, fin whale and sperm whale
